Check your understanding

How to study a reaction

1. Identify the functional group: C=C (count substituents), C≡C, C–X (methyl, 1°, 2°, 3°), or the oxygen function (alcohol, phenol, ether, epoxide, carbonyl, ester).
2. Read the reagent and conditions (strong/weak nucleophile or base, protic/aprotic solvent, heat, peroxides): acid (protonates O or C=C), base (deprotonates O–H), hydride or Grignard (attacks C=O), oxidant, or a reagent that turns OH into a leaving group (HX, PBr₃, SOCl₂, TsCl).
3. Decide the pathway (addition, Sₙ2, Sₙ1, E2, E1, radical chain) and follow every lone pair, π bond, charge and radical.
4. Rotate to inspect back-side attack (Sₙ2, epoxide opening), anti-periplanar H (E2) and the face of attack on C=O.
5. Predict connectivity and stereochemistry (inversion, retention, trans opening, racemic products, Zaitsev).
6. Compare the slide numbers shown under the title and reveal the answer.

Model conventions

Models prioritise bond connectivity and approach faces. Grouped substituents are not single atoms. sp carbons are linear (180°), sp² trigonal planar (120°) and sp³ tetrahedral (109.5°). Saturated six-membered rings are chairs, cyclopentane rings are puckered and acyclic sp³ C–C bonds are staggered. Sₙ2 and E2 transition states are drawn with partial (dashed) bonds; stereocentres are built with the configuration named in the text. Transition geometries remain illustrative rather than energy-minimised. Inter-stage motion is schematic; read the discrete stages for chemical species.

125 self-contained CHE 251 lessons: Reactions of alkenes, Unit 4.4 Alkynes, Unit 5 Alkyl halides, Unit 6 Alcohols and Unit 7 Ethers. No network connection or installation is required. 3D models were generated offline from explicit connectivity with a distance-geometry force field (ideal bond lengths, hybridisation angles, planarity/chirality and steric terms); transition-state geometries are illustrative.
